title: Output Is Where the Curves Cross

scenes.tts: At rest, each side of an adult human heart pumps about five litres of blood a minute. Over any few minutes, it cannot pump out more than flows back in. So what sets cardiac output? The heart, or the veins that fill it?
scenes.visual: A heart block and a veins block with an arrow of blood back in and an arrow of output out; a question mark over each; out is capped by in.
scenes.narration: At rest, each side of an adult human heart pumps about five litres of blood a minute. Over any few minutes, it cannot pump out more than flows back in. So what sets cardiac output? The heart, or the veins that fill it?

scenes.tts: The Fick principle is bookkeeping for oxygen. At steady state, the oxygen the lungs take up each minute leaves in the blood flowing through them. Take made up numbers for an adult at rest. Uptake is two hundred sixty millilitres of O two per minute. Arterial blood holds one hundred ninety five millilitres per litre. Mixed venous blood from the pulmonary artery holds one hundred forty three. The difference is fifty two. Two hundred sixty divided by fifty two is five litres per minute.
scenes.visual: A lungs block with uptake going in from below, mixed-venous blood in at the left and arterial blood out at the right; the numbers are subtracted and divided to give 5.0 L/min.
scenes.caption: The Fick principle is bookkeeping for oxygen. At steady state, the oxygen the lungs take up each minute leaves in the blood flowing through them. Take made-up numbers for an adult at rest. Uptake is 260 mL O2 per min. Arterial blood holds 195 mL per L. Mixed-venous blood from the pulmonary artery holds 143. The difference is 52. 260 divided by 52 is 5 L per min.

scenes.tts: Stop the heart, and the systemic circulation settles at one pressure. That zero flow pressure is the mean systemic filling pressure. In a tank, fluid below the outlet rim, the unstressed volume, fills it without stretching the walls. Fluid above the rim, the stressed volume, stretches them and pushes back. Adding blood raises the pressure. Guyton's group measured about six to seven millimetres of mercury in anaesthetized dogs, a dog value, not a normal human one.
scenes.visual: A stopped heart; a tank with a rim: unstressed volume below, stressed above, and a pressure bracket; adding blood raises the level.

scenes.tts: Guyton's group replaced the right heart with an external pump, in open chest dogs. They set right atrial pressure and measured the return. As they lowered the pressure, return rose along a roughly straight line. It stopped rising at about minus two to minus four millimetres of mercury, because veins collapse. Return reached zero where atrial pressure equals filling pressure. That line is the venous return curve. Flow equals filling pressure minus atrial pressure, divided by the resistance to venous return.
scenes.visual: Bypass strip, then axes: a dot moves along the venous return line to a collapse zone and back to zero flow; the equation appears.

Return reached zero where atrial pressure equals filling pressure. That line is the venous return curve. Flow equals filling pressure minus atrial pressure, divided by the resistance to venous return.

scenes.tts: The heart has a curve too. Higher atrial pressure fills the ventricle more, so output rises. Averaged over time, output equals venous return, so the circulation settles where the lines cross. This is an illustrative model, not fitted to data. Three plus atrial pressure equals seven minus atrial pressure. That gives atrial pressure two millimetres of mercury, output five litres per minute.
scenes.visual: The heart's line is drawn; the lines cross at a dot; the equation is solved and the operating point read off the axes.
scenes.caption: The heart has a curve too. Higher atrial pressure fills the ventricle more, so output rises. That gives atrial pressure 2 mmHg, output 5 L per min.

scenes.tts: In the model, move one line at a time. A stronger heart lifts its line. Output rises to six, and atrial pressure falls to one. A weaker heart drops it. Output falls to four, and atrial pressure rises to three. Over hours to days, venoconstriction and retained salt and water raise filling pressure to nine, and the veins' line slides right. Output is back to five, atrial pressure at four. The rule to keep: output sits where the heart's line crosses the veins' line.
scenes.visual: Three cases move one line each; the crossing dot and readout update and are cleared between cases; the rule ends the film.
